blocks.text: “He was almost recovered, but he has been greatly upset by Mr. Hawkins’s death.” He interrupted:—
“Oh, yes, I know, I know. I have read your last two letters.” I went on:—
“I suppose this upset him, for when we were in town on Thursday last he had a sort of shock.”
“A shock, so soon after brain fever! That was not good. What kind of a shock was it?”

“He thought he saw someone who reminded him of something terrible. It was something which had led to his brain fever.” At this point, all my feelings seemed to rush over me at once. I felt pity for Jonathan and the horror he had felt. There was the whole frightening mystery of his diary. There was also the fear that had hung over me ever since. All these feelings came together in wild confusion. I suppose I lost control of my feelings. I fell on my knees and held up my hands to him. I begged him to make my husband well again. He took my hands, helped me up, and made me sit on the sofa. He sat beside me and held my hand in his. Then he spoke to me with, oh, such endless kindness:—

“My life is empty and lonely, and so full of work. I have not had much time for friendships. But my friend John Seward called me here, and since then I have met so many good people. I have seen them show such goodness that I feel my loneliness more than ever. That feeling has grown as I have grown older. So believe me when I say that I come here full of respect for you. You have given me hope. It is not hope about what I am searching for. It is hope that there are still good women left to make life happy. Their lives and their honesty may teach good lessons to children yet to be born. I am glad, glad, that I may be able to help you here. If your husband is suffering, his suffering is something I have studied and have experience of. I promise that I will gladly do everything I can for him. I will do all I can to help him live as a strong man, and to make your life happy. Now you must eat. Your feelings have become too much for you, and perhaps you worry too much. Your husband Jonathan would not like to see you so pale. When he sees something he dislikes in someone he loves, it is not good for him. So, for his sake, you must eat and smile. You have told me all about Lucy. We shall not speak of it now, because it might upset you. I shall stay in Exeter tonight. I want to think carefully about what you have told me. After that, I will ask you questions, if I may. You will also tell me as much as you can about your husband Jonathan’s trouble. But not yet. You must eat now. Afterwards, you shall tell me everything.”
After lunch, when we went back to the sitting room, he said to me:—

“And now tell me all about him.” When I had to speak to this great man of learning, I began to feel afraid. He might think I was a weak fool and Jonathan was mad. Everything in that journal is so strange. I hesitated to go on. But he was so gentle and kind, and he had promised to help. I trusted him, so I said:—

“Dr. Van Helsing, what I have to tell you is very strange. You must not laugh at me or at my husband. Since yesterday, I have been full of doubts that leave me restless and upset. You must be kind to me. Do not think me foolish for even half believing some very strange things.” Both his manner and his words helped me feel less afraid when he said:—

“Oh, my dear, if you only knew how strange the matter that brought me here is! You would be the one to laugh. I have learned not to look down on anyone’s beliefs, however strange they may be. I have tried to keep an open mind. Ordinary things in life could not close it. But strange things could—the most unusual things, which make people wonder whether they are mad or sane.”
